title: Music and the Brain
objective: After this level you can explain what happens in the brain when we hear music.
summary: Hair cells send signals up the auditory nerve to the temporal lobes. A steady beat stirs movement areas, chills release dopamine, and the Mozart effect was brief.

cards.headline: Your favorite song and a good meal share a brain chemical.
cards.body: When a piece of music gives you chills, your brain releases dopamine, a chemical also involved in the pleasure of rewards like food. Scientists caught it happening in 2011. But before a song can thrill you, it has to get into your head at all. Let's follow it in.

cards.headline: Your ears collect the sound; your brain hears it
cards.body: Remember Level 10's cochlea, where hair cells sort pitch like keys along a piano? Those hair cells turn the vibration into an electrical signal. The auditory nerve carries that signal to the brain, and the brain turns it into a sound you recognize. Its receiving desk is an area at the top of each temporal lobe. Until the signal arrives there, a song is just a pattern of electricity.

cards.headline: Sitting still, part of you is dancing
cards.body: Hearing is only the start. In a 2007 brain-imaging study, listeners heard different rhythms while lying still. Rhythms with a regular beat, the steady pulse from Level 4, drove extra activity in movement areas of the brain: the basal ganglia and the supplementary motor area. Nobody was moving. So when you say a song makes you want to move, your brain agrees. It has already started.

cards.headline: The chills are chemistry
cards.body: Back to the hook. In that 2011 study, music that gave listeners chills released dopamine in the striatum, deep in the brain. The timing was the surprise. At the peak moment, the release centered on one region, the nucleus accumbens. In the run-up, while listeners anticipated the peak, it came from another, the caudate. Your brain pays out twice: once for the big moment, and once for the wait.

cards.fact: Playing Mozart won't make you smarter.
cards.context: In 1993, students did better on a spatial-reasoning task right after hearing a Mozart sonata, but the boost faded within about 15 minutes. A 2010 analysis of nearly 40 studies found little evidence of any special Mozart effect, and other music did about as well. Music does remarkable things in the brain; this just isn't one of them.

mascot.line: This is Level 38's myth again. Enjoy Mozart; just don't expect him to make you smarter.

cards.headline: Music and the brain: traced
learned: Hair cells make signals; the auditory nerve carries them to the brain
A steady beat stirs movement areas, even when you sit still
Chills release dopamine: in the wait and at the peak
The Mozart effect was brief and not special to Mozart

questions.prompt: In the 2011 brain-scan study of musical chills, which chemical was released at the peak moments?

options.label: Adrenaline
options.rationale: The study measured dopamine, the reward chemical.

options.label: Melatonin
options.rationale: That one is tied to sleep, not this study.

options.label: Insulin
options.rationale: A hormone for blood sugar, not a brain reward signal here.

questions.explanation: Pleasurable music that gave chills released dopamine in the striatum, a chemical also involved in rewards like food.

questions.prompt: You lie perfectly still listening to a song with a strong, regular beat. What did a 2007 brain-imaging study find in listeners like you?

options.label: Brain activity dropped overall
options.rationale: The beat drove extra activity, not less.

options.label: Memory areas switched off
options.rationale: The study found no such thing.

questions.explanation: Rhythms with a regular beat drove more activity in the basal ganglia and supplementary motor area, even with no movement.

questions.prompt: Following music from ear to brain, what carries the signal onward from the cochlea's hair cells?

options.label: The eardrum
options.rationale: The eardrum comes earlier, before the cochlea.

options.label: Air in the ear canal
options.rationale: Past the cochlea the signal is electrical.

options.label: The basal ganglia
options.rationale: That's a movement area deep in the brain.

questions.explanation: Hair cells turn vibration into an electrical signal, and the auditory nerve carries it to the brain.
